coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: Domestic work abroad is regulated via overseas-employment law (Proc. 923/2016 repealed and replaced by Proc. 1389/2025 per a Reporter/EBR summary; a Kuwait domestic-worker MoU ratified by Proc. 1337/2024). Buyer is the sending agency, not households. No household-employer registration duty found. See candidate on overseas employment agencies.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: No Ethiopian scrap-metal licensing law or register found in English search (results were Kenya, Zambia, UK). Nothing actionable; Amharic search not run.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: No Ethiopia-specific second-hand or pawn register found; only the general Addis Trade Bureau licence regime. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: Gold buying is channelled to the National Bank of Ethiopia (premium raised to 35%; officials want to cut out intermediary suppliers). No found record-keeping or reporting regime for jewellers. One weak candidate recorded.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: Nothing on dismantler or used-parts licensing found; only general trade licensing and annual renewal.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: 2014 live animals marketing law (licensed traders, registered markets) and a draft slaughter/traceability proclamation (status unconfirmed). Nothing new beyond K11 (ETLITS).

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: Study evidence of weak regulation and ~60-80% illegal slaughter in Addis; a Ministry of Agriculture draft proclamation would require sourcing from registered farm/market and slaughter in abattoirs (enactment unconfirmed). Weak candidate recorded.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No search spent; K05 already covers honey exporter traceability.

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: Proclamation 728/2011 governs veterinary drugs; Reg. 325/2014 sets fees; Ethiopian Agricultural Authority reportedly moved applications to an e-service system (Jan 2025 directive, per a 2025 report). Retail shop duties not confirmed.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Water Resources Management Proc. 197/2000 and Council of Ministers Reg. 115/2005 require permits, certification of drillers and drilling-completion reports to the supervising body. Current licensing process and any replacing law unconfirmed.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: Solid Waste Management Proc. 513/2007 lets private operators and MSEs hold collection permits; Addis zones assigned per enterprise. Nothing found on septic truck licensing.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: Ethiopian Construction Authority draft directive (Fortune, 27 Sep 2025) would license elevator installers, maintainers and independent inspection firms who issue clearance reports. No deadline, finalisation unconfirmed. Boiler and pressure-vessel rules not found.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: No dedicated search; only the general water-permit regime surfaced under category 10.

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: Fertilizer Proc. 137/1998 requires a competence certificate for wholesale or retail; Pesticide Decree 20/1990 (registration). Whether the Agricultural Authority now licenses dealers, and any 2024-25 change, not confirmed.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Overseas employment is under Proc. 1389/2025 (replacing 923/2016 as amended 1246/2021): agency capital 5m-20m Br and USD 50k-250k security deposit tiers (Oct 2025 Ministry of Labour and Skills directive), an Ethiopian Labour Migration Information System, and a 2024 licensing backlog of 100+ applicants. Candidate recorded.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: No search spent; K04 covers edir ledgers. See CSO candidate for the reporting regime that may apply to associations.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: CSO Proclamation 1113/2019: annual renewal with general-assembly-approved audit report; Authority revoked 1,718 licences in 2024 for missing reports. Candidate recorded. Halal supervision not searched.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: Addis Transport Bureau is drafting ride-hailing rules (terminals, mandatory GPS, vehicle identification); 44 registered ride-hailing companies, only 10-15 active. Annual vehicle inspection regime and minibus association rules not confirmed. Weak candidate recorded.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: 2025 income tax amendment (Proc. 1395/2025) dissolves Category C into B, taxing sub-2m Br turnover individuals on gross sales at 2-5%; Addis business licences must be renewed yearly (Proc. 686/2014 rules; only 72% of 384,000 complied in the 2025 fiscal year per a Trade Bureau report). Forex bureaus under NBE Directive FXD/01/2024 (5 licensed Oct 2024). Candidates recorded.

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: Private kindergartens and schools are evaluated and de-licensed by Addis education quality authority (824 evaluated, 11 revoked in 2021); Directive 206 of 1994/95 outdated per a 2022 parliamentary committee. Driving schools, day care, tattoo, small food producers and hunting outfitters: nothing found, not separately searched.

result.competitor: I found no lodging-tax-specific product, local guesthouse PMS vendor or city portal for this tax. Registration is in person. The Bureau's e-filing service, per Fortune's 2022 report, covered large taxpayers first and gave Category C a view-only Et-Tax platform with payment at a bank; its current scope is unverified. ETTA Solutions' Zoorya (an ERP/POS on Sunmi devices, reported as Revenue-certified) serves restaurants, not hotels. Hotels with a POS can add a tax line by reconfiguring it, and Fortune says hotels were already doing this. Small presumptive taxpayers are assessed on 70% of revenue, which lowers the need for detailed records. My Amharic searches returned only news, no vendors.
result.duty: Addis Ababa City Council Regulation No. 204/2026, ratified and published in the Negarit Gazeta (Capital, 10 Jul 2026). It sets a 5% municipal tax on the daily room rate before VAT; food, drinks and spa services are excluded. It covers 1-7 star hotels, unrated hotels, resorts, lodges, motels, pensions and guesthouses. Operators must register in person at their medium- or large-taxpayer branch office, keep a physical or digital guest register, and label invoices 'Lodging/Accommodation Municipal Tax'. Category A files monthly and remits within 30 days. For Category B, Capital says quarterly returns, while Fortune says monthly reporting with quarterly settlement. Small operators without records pay 5% on an assumed 70% of revenue. Late filing costs 5% per month, capped at 50%. Late remittance adds interest plus a 15% penalty, and fraud is prosecuted under the penal code. The Tourism Commission needs a tax-compliance letter before renewing accreditation or a licence. The start date is not settled: Fortune says 19 Jun 2026, Amharic sources via Ethiopanorama say Hamle 1, 2018 EC (about 8 Jul 2026), and a Marriott property notice says September 2026. I could not get the full gazette text. This is a city-level duty that is in force.
result.market: Fortune estimates 500+ bookable hotels in Addis with more than 25,000 rooms, and gives no count of guesthouses or pensions. A 2015 Ministry of Tourism figure puts all of Ethiopia at about 463 hotels; it is dated. I did not find a register count of unrated pensions or guesthouses, so that is unverified. At a guess the reachable market is a few hundred to a low few thousand establishments in one city.
result.reason: The duty is real and recurring, with monthly or quarterly returns, a guest register, an invoice label, and a compliance letter needed for licence renewal. Fortune reports that hotels were not ready. However, the core job is a single 5% line on room revenue that existing POS/ERP systems can be set up to add. Small operators without records are moved to a presumptive 70% revenue base. Registration and filing appear to happen in person at branch offices. The market is one city, with about 500 bookable hotels plus an unknown number of pensions, and willingness to pay among small guesthouses is likely low. A simple register-plus-return MVP is feasible and could be sold through the Hotel Owners Association, but it will struggle to stand alone apart from a broader PMS or e-invoicing bundle (related: K01).

result.competitor: I found no commercial landlord compliance or lease-registration software for Ethiopia; this rests on searches in English and Amharic. Registration is done in person at woreda housing offices and Addis Mesob centres. I found no online state portal, only a 2025 academic prototype (JESIT paper). The bureau says it has a central database of about 500,000 registered rentals. The real competition is free in-person registration plus the presumptive assessment the woreda carries out itself.
result.duty: The duty is real. Addis Ababa Directive No. 7/2024 has been in force since 30 May 2024, issued under Proclamation 1320/2024. It requires residential rent agreements to be registered and authenticated at sub-city or woreda housing offices, using a model contract with a minimum two-year term. Penalties under Art. 17 run from 1 to 3 months' rent. In 2026 the city ran a renewal drive: it opened in early July with an 11.25% rent cap, and the deadline was extended from 6 Aug to 5 Sep 2026. Renewals were done in person at woreda centres and Addis Mesob one-stop centres. The Revenue Bureau directive has its own rules, as reported by Addis Fortune: register every lease, collect rent only through bank or digital channels, a 35% flat deduction, surcharges of 5% to 25%, a 10% penalty for false declarations, and vacancy penalties. I did not find its number, its official text or any filing deadlines. The article's date is unclear: the search listing shows Jul 12, 2026, but an identical-text listing shows Oct 27, 2024, so it may be a re-run of a 2024 directive. Category C rental tax is presumptive and assessed by the woreda revenue office, so the landlord's filing work is small.
result.market: The bureau reports about 500,000 registered rental properties and lessors in its registry. In an earlier year the Revenue Bureau planned to collect rental income tax from 182,971 taxpayers (Fortune, 2023). The buyers are mostly individual households, not regulated businesses.
result.reason: The duty and penalties are real, and no competing software turned up. But the core job is an in-person visit with documents at a woreda or Mesob office, and the woreda assesses the presumptive Category C tax itself, so software has little to automate. Renewals are periodic, and the 2026 window closed on 5 Sep. The buyers are scattered individual landlords. Many of them under-report on purpose, so they have little reason to pay for help formalising. Payment and digital adoption are also hard. Fit with the study definition is borderline because these are households earning income, not businesses or employers. The Revenue Bureau directive's date and number are unconfirmed. A done-for-you agent service could exist, but its willingness to pay and scale look weak.

result.competitor: Coopbank of Oromia's SACCO-Link, a core banking product for cooperatives that covers member KYC, savings, loans and real-time financial reports. Search snippets mention 42 SACCOs and 10 unions onboarded; I could not open the page (503). Pitron FinOS, launched July 2026 and aimed at Ethiopian financial cooperatives, SACCOs and MFIs to replace paper processes (Capital Ethiopia). Vite Technologies (Addis Ababa) supports core banking for MFIs and SACCOs, based on a job posting. Amref/USAID Kefeta youth SACCO MIS with Awash Bank (2023). Generic SACCO systems such as Intelligrow. Adoption is still low: the 2026 Shega report says many cooperatives still keep manual records. I did not find a product focused on Commission audit preparation or reporting, but bookkeeping and member ledgers, the core job, are already contested by a bank-backed product.
result.duty: The duty is real and in force, but the claim misstates where it comes from. Cooperatives are registered and regulated under Cooperative Societies Proclamation 985/2016, with the Federal Cooperative Agency/Commission or a regional body as the authority. The Ethiopian Cooperative Commission's Cooperative Societies Audit Implementation Directive No. 978/2016 (Ethiopian calendar, dated December 2023) sets up audits at least once a year, including delegated audits, and a complaint process for audit reports. So the annual audit does not depend on the draft amendment. The draft amendment, still under review in Parliament and not confirmed as enacted, would require an annual general assembly and an annual audit, allow non-members up to 10% of capital, and let officials set financial inspection standards. Enforcement is weak: The Reporter says only about 20% of cooperatives had been audited, and the Commission planned to outsource audits because it lacks auditors. I could not open the directive PDF (HTTP 503), so I have not confirmed specific penalties, filing deadlines or report formats.
result.market: A 2021 Ethiopian Cooperative Commission report, cited in a journal article, counts 92,755 cooperatives, of which 21,328 are SACCOs with 5.38M members and 18.54B ETB in savings and shares. Addis Fortune (Feb 2024) says the ECC directive covers about 23,000 cooperatives doing financial services. Capital Ethiopia (2026) cites more than 18,000 SACCOs and MFIs. Most are small and rural, with low digital literacy, so they have little ability to pay.
result.reason: The annual audit duty is real (Audit Directive 978/2016 EFY under Proclamation 985/2016), but enforcement is weak (about 20% audited), and the amendment the claim relies on is still a draft. Bookkeeping and member ledgers, the core job, are already offered by Coopbank of Oromia's SACCO-Link (a bank-backed product, likely bundled), Pitron FinOS (2026), Vite Technologies and NGO-funded MIS. Buyers are about 21,000 mostly rural SACCOs with low digital literacy and little ability to pay. Banks and NGOs control distribution. A gap may remain for an audit-preparation or Commission-reporting add-on, but I could not confirm report formats. Low score: weak willingness to pay, existing bank-backed competitors, hard distribution.

result.competitor: No Ethiopian software found for controlled-drug registers or reporting. MedRafa (Addis Ababa startup) onboards pharmacies to a general inventory management system. EFDA eRIS (i-License, i-Register, i-Import) covers licensing, registration and imports; I found no evidence of a pharmacy dispensing or narcotic register module. Public facilities use the SIAPS/MoH electronic dispensing tool (EDT); it doesn't cover private retail.
result.duty: EFDA Narcotic and Psychotropic Medicine Control Directive No. 1121/2018 EC (Dec 2025), issued under Proclamation 1112/2019. The text couldn't be read: the PDF is encoded Ge'ez and the fetch tool couldn't decode it. Per Addis Fortune: pharmacies handling controlled medicines must keep separate storage, registry systems and accountability mechanisms; need specific EFDA competency certification; may list only one controlled drug per prescription form; inspectors can audit stock, suspend licences, confiscate medicines and prosecute; penalties sharply increased. Per PMC9016557 (earlier regulation): wholesalers and dispensers must report narcotic stock status every 3 months. Not found: whether e-reporting is mandated, the register format, and the exact report frequency under 1121.
result.market: About 618 pharmacies nationwide, more than half in Addis (Addis Fortune, 2025). Older EFMHACA figures: 377 pharmacies, 1,699 drug shops and 1,392 rural drug vendors; drug shops and rural vendors generally can't stock narcotics. A 2024 national list limits which facilities may dispense narcotics and psychotropics, so the addressable market is likely a few hundred pharmacies plus hospital and clinic pharmacies. The exact number authorized for controlled drugs was not found.
result.reason: The duty is real. Under EFDA Directive 1121/2018 EC (Dec 2025), pharmacies need separate storage and registry systems for controlled medicines, separate EFDA competency certification, and face stock audits, licence suspension and court action. Earlier rules already required wholesalers and dispensers to report stock quarterly. I couldn't parse the directive PDF, so the register format and any e-reporting mandate are unverified. No Ethiopian product does controlled-drug registers. MedRafa sells general pharmacy inventory software in Addis. Market is small: about 618 pharmacies (Addis Fortune 2025), and a 2024 national list restricts which facilities may dispense narcotics. Only 15 of 22 stocking pharmacies filed the quarterly report, so enforcement is weak. Low willingness to pay; a paper register is enough.

The duty is only a Ministry of Agriculture draft. I found no evidence it was enacted or has an effective date. The Reporter says the draft would criminalise slaughter outside abattoirs for retail (up to 3 years in prison, fine of at least 20,000 Br) and would require slaughter livestock to come from a registered farm or market. The 300,000 Br fine in the sources applies to export slaughter and quarantine, not to butchers. I found no butcher-registration or slaughter-record provision. Current rules are city-level bans. The buyers are fragmented informal butchers, and any traceability would run through the state ETLITS system (K11). I did not search for market size or for competing products. Score is low.

The duty is real. PEA notices (2022 delivery reporting, 2023 inventory reporting with licence revocation) and mandatory digital payment via Telebirr, CBE or Coop are all reported. The audits are real too: 40 stations were suspended in 2023, and 13 distributors were disciplined in July 2025. But the core job is already done by a state system. Ethio telecom built a government fuel supply-chain platform with PEA, the Trade Ministry and EPSE, covering trucks from Djibouti through to the pump, with station data feeding PEA directly. A national fuel aggregator portal, with M-Pesa folded in and built by EagleLion Systems under the Ministry of Transport and Logistics, plans smart terminals for inventory tracking. Stations are mostly owned by oil companies, so buyers are few and large, and the state owns the reporting channel. I did not find any 2026 sources on the market size, and I did not check the emergency directive's text.
